weakness: The program released the object exactly where it had picked it up and never told the planner about other objects. With a low wall between the robot and the object, the horizontal hand and forearm needed for the upright release collided with the wall, knocking the object away (6/10 failures). A second, latent weakness surfaced while repairing: the object pivoted in the fingers during the reorienting swing, so the hand-to-object transform measured before the swing was stale at release.
how_found: Listed every motion and asked what volume it sweeps. The release pose puts the hand and forearm horizontally beside the object, a volume that is never checked, and the release spot was copied from the pick spot as if free space there were guaranteed. Clutter between a robot and its target is common on real tables. (Moving the object far forward or sideways, the first idea, did not break the program: reach was not the weak point.)
why_missed: In the default scene the table is empty, so every pose the planner could reach was also collision-free; the program was written for the empty scene and the success rate gave no signal that the free-space assumption existed.
fix: Read get_obstacles() at the start and pass every non-target object as avoid= to every move_to; raise the transport height above the tallest obstacle; choose the release spot from a ranked set of nearby candidates whose footprint is clear and let the obstacle-aware planner reject the ones where the arm does not fit; retreat upward if backing out is blocked. Re-measure the held object's pose in the hand after the swing and correct the hand pose before the final release.
general_rule: Plan every motion, including the place/release pose and the retreat, against the obstacles you perceive, and treat the place location as a choice to be checked for free space for the whole arm rather than assuming the pick location is free.

weakness: The program had exactly one grasp point (a fixed offset along the object). A second object standing 1 cm beside the object at that point left no room for a finger, so the obstacle-aware planner (correctly) refused the grasp on every attempt and the program gave up (0/10), even though most of the object's length was free.
how_found: After round 1 the program passed obstacles to the planner, so I asked what it would do when the planner says no: every fallback (retry) re-tried the same grasp point. Before choosing this, motion (sliding peg up to ~11 cm/s), mass/friction (2-3 kg, mu 0.1-0.5) and yaw (45/90 deg) were screened and did not break it (0.6-1.0), because the retry loop and the across-the-object grasp already tolerated them.
why_missed: On an empty table any grasp point works, so a single hard-coded offset never failed; the round-1 obstacle fix only added a check (planner rejection) without adding alternatives to fall back on.
fix: Generate several grasp points along the object's long axis, prefilter each by checking that both open fingers' volumes are clear of the (averaged) obstacle boxes, and take the first that the obstacle-aware planner can reach; decide which end goes up after the grasp from reachability (hand pointing away from the robot, hand above the object's centre) instead of from which half was grasped; average 20 obstacle readings instead of using one noisy reading.
general_rule: Every collision check you add must come with a set of alternatives (grasp points, approach directions, place spots) to try when it rejects the default, and the grasp must be chosen by checking that the gripper's own volume (open fingers) fits next to the object's neighbours.

weakness: The program assumed unlimited headroom: it lifted to 'above every obstacle top', used a vertical hand whose wrist needs ~0.3 m above the grasp, never checked whether a motion actually arrived, and ignored the held/standing object in planning. Under a shelf 0.39 m above the table the arm started pressed against the shelf (every plan refused), the vertical grasp did not fit, the lift sent the held peg into the shelf, pitched grasps stalled on contact and then closed anyway, and retreats routed around the shelf swept through the standing peg.
how_found: After rounds 1-2 the program reasoned about obstacles beside the object; I asked what it assumed above it. The lift height rule 'max(obstacle tops) + margin' only makes sense when nothing hangs overhead.
why_missed: Every earlier scene had open space above, so 'go higher to be safe' was always right; the planner hides collisions of anything it is not told about (the held object, the placed object) and returns success for plans that contact stops short.
fix: Kept (they do not hurt other scenes): escape move when the start state is in contact; vertical corridor (floor/ceiling) from obstacles near the object; lift heights tried from high to low under the ceiling; pitched hand approaches (60/45 deg) as alternatives to the vertical one with depth reduced so the palm clears the object; check the TCP actually reached the grasp pose before closing; release spots searched up to 0.3 m towards the robot; retreat planned with the placed object as an obstacle. Not enough: 0.1 -> 0.6. Remaining failures are random: the RRT fallback often finds long detours under the shelf, and the peg (invisible to the planner while held) is sometimes flung or snagged during the swing.
why_unsolved: In this confined space the program's single manipulation strategy (pick, swing upright in the air, lower) needs a large free volume for the arm plus the held object, and the planner cannot account for the held object. A reliable solution would need a different strategy (e.g. pivot the peg upright against the table without lifting it, or slide it out from under the shelf first) or a planner that models the grasped object; six local repairs could not get there. The official oracle also scores 0/10.
general_rule: Derive clearance from the actual free space in every direction (including overhead) instead of 'higher is safer', and never trust a planner's success for things it does not model: verify that each motion arrived, and treat held and just-placed objects as obstacles you must account for yourself.

s0_note: gate re-measured s0 of the frozen (post-round-3) pipeline as 0.7; 20-seed check gave 0.85, traced to retreat moves (fixed this round)
weakness: The program looked at the scene once per attempt and then executed open-loop: the release spot was chosen before the long swing and never re-checked, so a box that slid into the work area during the swing ended up under the peg, and the peg was stood on top of the box (9/10 failures). Repairs also exposed that hovering only ~1 cm above possible obstacles let a moving object hit the held peg, and that a retreat planned with the standing peg in the avoid list started inside its inflated box and made the planner detour through it.
how_found: After round 3 the program reasoned carefully about static obstacles, so I asked how old that information was by the time it acted: obstacles were read at the start of the attempt, about 10 s before the release. In a shared workspace (people, other robots, conveyors) the scene changes in that time.
why_missed: In every earlier scene the world was static apart from the robot, so perceiving once per attempt was indistinguishable from perceiving before every step.
fix: Re-read obstacles right before committing to the release; if anything moved more than 2 cm since the attempt started, hold still until it comes to rest; if the release spot is now occupied, carry the peg at a height where its bottom clears every obstacle top to the nearest free spot. Hover 10 cm above the table (instead of 3-6 cm) until that final check, then descend. Retreat: a short straight back-off without the peg in avoid (fingers slide off it), then further moves with the peg as an obstacle; if the back-off is refused, stay put.
general_rule: Perceive again immediately before every irreversible or contact-making step (grasp, release, insertion) and compare with what you planned on; if something moved, wait for it to settle and replan, and keep held objects well clear of surfaces until that final check.

weakness: Every grasp the program knew straddled the object with open fingers. With the object lying 1 cm from a low wall along its whole length, no grasp point had room for a finger, the program correctly rejected them all and then simply gave up (0/10), although the object could easily have been slid along the wall to where a grasp fits. The oracle also scored 0/10.
how_found: After round 2 the program had alternatives for where to grasp, so I asked what it does when every alternative is rejected: it returns 'unreachable'. All its alternatives assumed the object stays where it is. Objects pressed against bin walls, tray rims or other objects are common in real clutter. Heavy, slippery, rolled, leaning and near/far objects were screened first and did not break it (0.6-1.0); only masses above a real arm's payload did.
why_missed: On an open table some grasp always fits, and the round-2 fix only added more grasps of the same kind, all on the object as it lies. Changing the object's situation before grasping was never part of the plan.
fix: If no grasp fits anywhere along the object, predict how far it must be pushed along its own axis (in each direction, checking that its path is clear and it stays in reach) until a grasp would fit, preferring pushes towards the robot. Push it with the closed fingers against an end face: try a few start gaps and heights and let the obstacle-aware planner reject those where the palm hits the wall; plan the push without the object (the planner must not avoid what it is pushing), push 4 cm past the predicted minimum to absorb the contact gap, then retreat, look again and count the push only if the object actually moved; then grasp as usual (up to 3 pushes per run).
general_rule: When no grasp fits the object where it lies, do not give up: change its situation with a non-prehensile action (push or slide it through free space to where a grasp fits), predicted from the perceived free space and confirmed by looking again afterwards.

parameter_tuning_note: gate auto-check flagged true (same edit keys as v5: object_pose + add_obstacle); the variation attacks a different assumption (support height, not a wall beside the object). Tuning streak before was 0.
weakness: The free-space check for the open fingers swept a volume from the table (z = 0) up, i.e. it silently assumed the object rests on the table. With the object lying on a 4 cm platform, the platform itself filled that volume at every grasp point, so every grasp was rejected and the program gave up at once (0/10), although the fingers never come near the platform. The release search also only looked within 0.30 m, too close to leave a large support.
how_found: Read every geometric check and asked which numbers are world constants rather than measured: the finger box's lower bound was a hard-coded 0.0. Objects on real robots are often picked from boxes, shelves or pallets rather than from the surface the task ends on.
why_missed: Every earlier scene had the object on the table, so 'down to the table' and 'down to the object's bottom' were the same number; the check was written in world coordinates instead of relative to the object.
fix: Sweep the finger volume from the object's perceived bottom face up (not from z = 0), and search release spots in a wider area (up to 0.40 m back and 0.35 m to the sides) so a spot beside a large support is found.
general_rule: Express every geometric check relative to what you perceive (the object's own extent and the surface it actually rests on), never relative to a hard-coded world height or reference surface, or a scene that differs only in that reference will make the check reject everything.
